nindian-history-131-19.s: In which year was the Regulating Act passed?
nindian-history-131-19.x: The Regulating Act was passed in 1773; Pitt's India Act came in 1784, the Charter Act in 1813 and the Government of India Act in 1858.

nindian-history-131-8.s: Which of the following event–year pairs is NOT correctly matched?
nindian-history-131-8.x: The Battle of Buxar was fought in 1764; 1757 is the year of Plassey.

na80a126f160.s:
Consider the following statements about land revenue in Andhra:
1. The Mahalwari-type arrangement is associated with Nellore.
2. The Mahalwari-type arrangement is associated with Vizianagaram and Bobbili.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
na80a126f160.x: The Mahalwari-type arrangement is placed in Nellore (with Chittoor in some accounts); Vizianagaram and Bobbili were zamindaris under the Permanent Settlement.

nb0a3d9b394d.s:
Consider the following statements about the Mahalwari system:
1. Its common ownership arrangement was called Bhai Chara.
2. Its common ownership arrangement was also called Mahali.
3. Its common ownership arrangement was called Peshkash.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
nb0a3d9b394d.x: Common ownership under the Mahalwari framework was called Bhai Chara or Mahali; Peshkash was the fixed payment of zamindars.

n7e46526cc19.s: Whose canal project was a notable relief effort during the Great Madras Famine of 1876–78?
n7e46526cc19.x: Missionary John Clough's canal relief project was a notable response to the 1876–78 famine, whose laissez-faire relief worsened it.

new.s: The Charter Act of 1793 renewed the Company's charter for:
new.x: The Charter Act of 1793 renewed the charter and the trade monopoly for 20 years.

new.s: Under the Charter Act of 1793, the salaries of the Board of Control members were paid from:
new.x: The 1793 Act charged Board of Control members' salaries to Indian revenues.

new.s: Which Charter Act renewed the Company's authority with no fixed term?
new.x: The Charter Act of 1853, the last one, renewed the Company's authority without fixing a term.

new.s: The sovereignty of the British Crown over the Company's Indian possessions was first asserted by the Charter Act of:
new.x: The Charter Act of 1813 asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown over the Company's Indian possessions.

new.s: Which Charter Act ended the Company's commercial functions and made it a purely administrative body?
new.x: The 1833 Act ended the Company's commercial rights, leaving it purely administrative, and let Europeans settle freely.

new.s: Evangelical pressure for missionaries' entry under the Charter Act of 1813 came from William Wilberforce and:
new.x: William Wilberforce and Charles Grant led the Evangelical pressure that got missionaries admitted in 1813.

new.s:
Consider the following statements about the Charter Act of 1813:
1. It provided an education grant of Rs 10 lakh a year.
2. It allowed missionaries to enter India and preach.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
new.x: The 1813 grant was Rs 1 lakh a year, not Rs 10 lakh; missionaries were allowed to enter and preach.

new.s: Who was the first Governor-General of India under the Charter Act of 1833?
new.x: The 1833 Act made the GG of Bengal the GG of India; Lord William Bentinck was the first, and also the last GG of Bengal.

new.s: Under the Charter Act of 1833, the Law Member was added to the Governor-General's Council as its:
new.x: The Law Member was the fourth member of the Council; the Act did not provide for an Indian Law Member.

new.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Charter Act of 1833?
o: The Governor-General of Bengal became Governor-General of India
Laws made by the Governor-General-in-Council were called Acts
It provided for an Indian Law Member
The Presidencies lost their law-making powers
new.x: The 1833 Act added a Law Member (Macaulay) but did not provide for an Indian Law Member.

new.s: Under the Charter Act of 1853, how many new legislative members were added to the Governor-General's Council?
new.x: Six legislative members were added, making a Central Legislative Council of 12 members in all.

new.s: Besides four provincial representatives, the new legislative members under the Charter Act of 1853 included one Calcutta Supreme Court judge and the:
new.x: The six were four provincial appointees, the Chief Justice and one Supreme Court judge; the Commander-in-Chief was not among them.

new.s: The Central Legislative Council created by the Charter Act of 1853 is often described as a:
new.x: With legislative functions separated and provincial members added, the 1853 Council worked as a 'mini-Parliament'.

new.s: The provinces represented among the new legislative members of 1853 were Madras, Bombay, Bengal and:
new.x: The four provincial members came from Madras, Bombay, Bengal and Agra.

new.s: The First Law Commission headed by Macaulay functioned during:
new.x: Macaulay headed the First Law Commission (1834–38), which drafted the Indian Penal Code.

new.s: Who first demanded the appointment of Indians in the services, in 1832?
new.x: Raja Ram Mohan Roy first demanded Indians in the services in 1832.

new.s: Fort William College, founded by Wellesley in 1800, was replaced for training civil servants by Haileybury in:
new.x: Fort William College (1800) gave way to Haileybury College in 1806.

new.s: Which Act reversed the centralising trend by restoring legislative power to Bombay and Madras?
new.x: The Indian Councils Act of 1861 restored law-making power to Bombay and Madras, beginning decentralisation.

new.s: The 'final step towards centralisation', giving the Governor-General-in-Council exclusive legislative power, was the:
new.x: The Charter Act of 1833 gave the GG-in-Council exclusive legislative power for all British India, the peak of centralisation.

new.s: Ryotwari was extended in the Bombay Presidency by:
new.x: Mountstuart Elphinstone extended Ryotwari in Bombay; Munro is linked with the Ceded Districts and Read with Baramahal.

new.s: Under which Regulation did Holt Mackenzie propose the Mahalwari system in 1822?
new.x: Mackenzie's proposal came under Regulation VII of 1822; Regulation IX of 1833 was Bird's revision.

new.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the land revenue system in the areas named?
new.x: Madras and Coorg came under Ryotwari, not the Permanent Settlement.

new.s: Under the Ryotwari system, revenue was periodically revised about every:
new.x: Ryotwari assessments were revised about every 30 years, unlike the permanently fixed zamindari demand.

new.s: Under the Permanent Settlement, the owner (proprietor) of the land was the:
new.x: The zamindar was the proprietor under the Permanent Settlement; the ryot under Ryotwari and the village jointly under Mahalwari.

new.s: Under the Permanent Settlement, the rights of zamindars were:
new.x: Zamindars were recognised as proprietors with hereditary, transferable and saleable rights.

new.s: The Haftam and Panjam regulations, which let zamindars seize tenants' property, were issued respectively in:
new.x: Haftam came in 1799 and Panjam in 1812.

new.s: Which was a drawback of the fixed revenue demand of the Permanent Settlement for the Company?
o: It could not gain from later price rises
new.x: The fixed demand gave sure income at low cost but did not let the Company gain from later price rises.

new.s: The first Ryotwari revenue demand was fixed at what share of the estimated produce?
new.x: The first Ryotwari demand was 50% of estimated produce, not 30%.

new.s:
Consider the following statements about the Ryotwari system:
1. Lands were surveyed and assessed before taxing.
2. The ryot could sell, mortgage or lease land while the assessment was paid.
3. Revenue was fixed permanently at a low rate.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
new.x: Ryotwari lands were surveyed first and the ryot could sell or mortgage land; revenue was often heavy and periodically revised, not fixed low.

new.s: The first Ryotwari experiment in the Madras Presidency was made in Baramahal in 1792 by:
new.x: Captain Alexander Read began the Baramahal experiment in 1792, assisted by Munro.

new.s: Ryotwari was generally adopted across the Madras Presidency in:
new.x: General adoption in Madras came in 1820, with Munro as Governor.

new.s: Which of the following was NOT part of the Baramahal area?
new.x: Baramahal covered Salem, Krishnagiri, Dharmapuri and Tiruvannamalai; Anantapur was Munro's HQ in the Ceded Districts.

new.s: During 1814–18, Thomas Munro served as:
new.x: Munro was President of the Judicial Commission in 1814–18 and Governor of Madras in 1820–27.

new.s: Thomas Munro is called the:
o: Father of land settlement in north India
new.x: Munro, who spread Ryotwari across Madras as Governor, is called the 'Father of Ryotwari'; Bird is the father of land settlement in north India.

new.s: Thomas Munro suppressed the Palegars of Rayalaseema with the help of officer:
new.x: Munro crushed the Rayalaseema palegars with officer Campbell.

new.s: Who revised the Mahalwari system under Regulation IX of 1833 and is called the 'father of land settlement in north India'?
new.x: R.M. Bird revised the system in 1833 with a survey-based settlement.

new.s: Who carried on R.M. Bird's settlement in the North-Western Provinces as Lieutenant-Governor?
new.x: James Thomason continued Bird's settlement in the NWP.

new.s: The Taluqdari system is associated with:
new.x: Taluqdari belongs to Awadh (Oudh); 'Taluqdari – Bombay' is a wrong pair.

new.s: The Northern Circars were obtained by the Company in:
new.x: The Northern Circars came in 1765–66 by Mughal farman and treaty with the Nizam; Guntur followed in 1788.

new.s: Guntur was acquired by the Company in:
new.x: Guntur was acquired in 1788; the Ceded Districts came in 1800.

new.s: The Battle of Padmanabham (1794) saw the defeat of which Vizianagaram zamindar?
new.x: At Padmanabham in 1794 the Vizianagaram zamindar Vijayarama Gajapati Raju was defeated.

new.s: In the Andhra revenue system, Moturpha was a tax on:
new.x: Moturpha was levied on professions, trades and looms of weavers, artisans and merchants.

new.s: In the Andhra revenue system, 'Haveli' land meant land:
new.x: Haveli was land under direct Company control; such lands were later brought under Ryotwari.

new.s: Under the mootah arrangement after 1802, many mootahdars:
new.x: Haveli lands grouped as mootahs and auctioned to mootahdars largely fell into arrears.

new.s: The Madras Inam Commission of 1858 was set up to check:
new.x: The 1858 Inam Commission examined titles to rent-free inam lands.

new.s: The cotton slump that led to defaults and loss of land to moneylenders followed the:
new.x: The cotton slump after the American Civil War led to defaults and land passing to moneylenders.

new.s: The new class that emerged in Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas was that of:
new.x: Moneylender-landlords rose in Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas; merchant-landlords in zamindari areas.

new.s: The free trade (industrial capital) stage of colonialism in India covered the period:
new.x: R.P. Dutt's free-trade stage ran 1813–1858, after the mercantilist stage (1757–1813).

new.s: R.P. Dutt set out the stages of colonialism in his book:
o: Poverty and Un-British Rule in India
new.x: R.P. Dutt proposed the three stages in India Today; Economic History of India is by R.C. Dutt.

new.s: The book 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901) was written by:
new.x: Dadabhai Naoroji wrote Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901).

new.s: 'Economic History of India' (1901–03) was written by:
new.x: R.C. Dutt wrote the two-volume Economic History of India; R.P. Dutt wrote India Today.

new.s: Which pair of author and book is correctly matched?
o: M.G. Ranade – Economic History of India
R.C. Dutt – Essays on Indian Economics
new.x: Digby wrote 'Prosperous' British India (1901); Ranade wrote Essays on Indian Economics and R.C. Dutt Economic History of India.

new.s: 'Some Economic Aspects of British Rule in India' (1903) was written by:
new.x: G. Subramania Iyer wrote it in 1903, presenting India as a supplier of cheap raw materials.

new.s: The term 'moral drain' was coined by:
new.x: Dadabhai Naoroji coined 'moral drain'.

new.s: Which was the largest single head of the British Indian budget?
new.x: Military expenditure on the British Indian Army and imperial wars was the largest single budget head.

new.s: According to Dadabhai Naoroji, the cause of the drain was:
o: Profits taken by British capitalists from India
new.x: Naoroji traced the drain to profits of British capitalists; the drain was not an excess of imports.

new.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the drain of wealth?
o: It took the form of an excess of imports
India generally had a favourable balance of trade
It began with the Diwani of Bengal
new.x: The drain took the form of unrequited exports, not an excess of imports.

new.s: 'Imperial preference' meant:
o: Higher duties on British imports in India
Lower duties for British imports in India
Free entry of Indian goods into Britain
new.x: Imperial preference gave British imports special privileges such as lower duties in India.

new.s: The Suez Canal, which tightened British control over Indian trade, was opened in:
new.x: The Suez Canal opened in 1869.

new.s: Lancashire cloth first reached Bengal in:
new.x: Lancashire cloth came to Bengal in 1786; calicoes were displaced by 1793.

new.s: By 1850, India took what share of all British cotton exports?
new.x: After 1813's one-way free trade, India took one-fourth of British cotton exports by 1850.

new.s: The list of causes of Indian deindustrialisation including transit duties and British privileges was given by:
new.x: B.D. Basu listed the causes: trade policy, raw-material export, duties, British privileges and railways.

new.s: Uppada is known for:
new.x: Uppada is known for jamdani silk; Eluru for carpets, Kurnool for blankets, Nellore for towels.

new.s: Which of the following place–product pairs is NOT correctly matched?
new.x: Ponduru is known for fine hand-spun khadi, not iron and steel.

new.s: Machilipatnam's famous painted cloth of the 16th–17th centuries was:
new.x: Machilipatnam was famed for chintz (painted cloth), dyed fabrics and muslins.

new.s: The main tea-growing region under British rule was:
new.x: Tea was grown mainly in Assam; jute in Bengal, cotton in the Deccan, Gujarat and Berar.

new.s: The Punjab Land Alienation Act of 1900 checked land transfer from agriculturists to:
new.x: The Act stopped land passing from agriculturists to non-agriculturists such as moneylenders.

new.s: The Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act of 1879 protected peasants against:
new.x: It protected peasants against moneylenders after the Deccan riots of 1875.

new.s: The famine commission appointed in 1866 after the Orissa famine was headed by:
new.x: The Campbell Commission of 1866 followed the Orissa famine; Strachey's came in 1880.

new.s: Which famine commission was set up in 1901 under Curzon?
new.x: The MacDonnell Commission came in 1901 under Curzon; Lyall's in 1897–98.

new.s: The Guntur famine of 1832–33 led to the building of which work by Arthur Cotton?
new.x: The Guntur famine prompted Arthur Cotton's Godavari anicut (1847–52).

new.s: The first attempt at a cotton mill in India, which failed, was made in 1818 at:
new.x: Fort Gloster (Kolkata) in 1818 failed; the first successful mill came in Bombay in 1854.

new.s: TISCO was incorporated in:
new.x: TISCO was incorporated in 1907 at Jamshedpur.

new.s: Which of the following is correct about ownership of mills in colonial India?
o: Cotton and jute mills were both Indian-owned
Cotton mills were foreign-owned; jute mills Indian-owned
Cotton mills were Indian-owned; jute mills foreign-owned
new.x: Cotton mills (Maharashtra, Gujarat) were Indian-owned; jute mills (Bengal) were foreign-owned.

new.s: Against the Hilton Young ratio of 1s 6d, Indian business led by Purshottamdas Thakurdas wanted the rupee at:
new.x: Indian business wanted 1s 4d; the Commission fixed 1s 6d.

new.s: The Hilton Young Commission recommended a central bank, which led to the RBI in:
new.x: Its central-bank proposal led to the Reserve Bank of India in 1935.

new.s: The per capita income of India in 1947 was about:
new.x: Per capita income on the eve of independence was about Rs 265 a year; Rs 20 was Naoroji's 1867–68 estimate.

new.s: On the eve of independence, the literacy rate in India was:
new.x: Literacy was under 16% (female under 9%); 32 years was life expectancy.

new.s: On the eve of independence, basic and capital goods formed about what share of industrial output?
new.x: India lacked a capital-goods base: basic and capital goods were only about one-fourth of industrial output.
